message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ URL parser library **purely as a black box**.

The only artifact is the compiled binary: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable
There is NO library source available anywhere on disk (do not go looking for url_parser.h/.cpp — it does not exist). Do not try to disassemble or run 'strings'. Use ONLY behavioral probing: run the binary with argument values and observe stdout.

Usage: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "<url>"
With fewer than 2 argv entries it returns exit code 1 and prints nothing.

It prints EXACTLY 18 lines, in this order (one per line, via std::cout << x << std::endl):
 1  scheme()          (string)
 2  authority()       (string)
 3  userinfo()        (string)
 4  host()            (string)
 5  port()            (int, prints -1 when absent)
 6  path()            (string)
 7  query()           (string)
 8  fragment()        (string)
 9  has_scheme()      (bool printed as 1/0)
10  has_authority()
11  has_userinfo()
12  has_host()
13  has_port()
14  has_path()
15  has_query()
16  has_fragment()
17  to_string()       (string)
18  is_valid()        (bool 1/0)

A labeled probe helper already exists at /tmp/probe.sh (takes any number of url args). If missing, recreate it:

  cat > /tmp/probe.sh << 'EOS'
  #!/bin/bash
  LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
  for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
    mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
    for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"; done
  done
  EOS
  chmod +x /tmp/probe.sh

Note: /tmp/probe.sh renders empty fields as []. For inputs containing characters bash would mangle, invoke the binary directly with careful quoting, or use printf/hexdump to inspect raw bytes:
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$URL" | od -c | head -40

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verified; you may re-verify but do not spend most of your budget here):
- A scheme is recognized ONLY when the literal "://" appears. "mailto:user@example.com" yields NO scheme and the entire input becomes path. "//example.com/path" yields no scheme and the whole thing is path (authority is parsed only when "://" was found).
- scheme() is LOWERCASED ("HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM" -> scheme "http"), but host() case is preserved ("EXAMPLE.COM").
- authority() is RECONSTRUCTED from userinfo/host/port, not the raw substring: "http://example.com:80abc" -> authority "example.com:80"; "http://example.com:" -> authority "example.com".
- port parsing behaves like std::stoi + a range check: "80abc"->80, "+80"->80, " 80"->80, "065"->65, "0"->0, but "-80"->absent, "65536"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "abc"->absent, ""->absent. Absent port prints -1 with has_port 0 and is omitted from authority()/to_string().
- Splitting after authority: the FIRST '#' splits off fragment (so "#a#b" -> fragment "a#b"); then within the part BEFORE that '#', the FIRST '?' splits off query. "/p#a?b" -> fragment "a?b", no query.
- has_*() appear to be "field is non-empty" for strings ("http://example.com/#" -> fragment "" and has_fragment 0), and has_port() is port != -1. BUT has_authority() is NOT simply "authority string non-empty": "http://:8080" gives authority ":8080" yet has_authority 0 (host is empty there) — pin down the real rule.
- No path normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding ("%7E" preserved).
- is_valid(): "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, but "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.

YOUR JOB: exhaustively probe your assigned family below. Run MANY probes (dozens — at least 40 distinct inputs; more is better). For every behavior you claim, you MUST have run the exact input. Derive precise, implementable rules (as if writing pseudocode), and explicitly flag anything ambiguous or surprising.

Return findings as structured output. Rules must be stated so a programmer can implement them without further probing. Include the concrete probe evidence (input -> the specific field values that matter) for each rule. Prefer many small precise rules over few vague ones.

YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY:
PATH / QUERY / FRAGMENT SPLITTING.
Confirm and refine the ordering rule (first '#' splits fragment; then first '?' in the remainder splits query). Probe with and without a scheme/authority. Critical: do '?' and '#' appearing INSIDE the authority region terminate the authority? e.g. "http://example.com?q=1" (already known: authority example.com, query q=1), "http://ex.com#f", "http://u@ex.com?x", "http://ex.com:80?x", "http://ex.com:80#f", "http://ex.com?x:80" — does the authority end at the first of '/', '?', '#'? Probe "http://ex.com" vs "http://ex.com/" (path "/" vs ""). Empty pieces: "http://ex.com/?#", "http://ex.com/#?", "http://ex.com?#", "http://ex.com#?", "?q=1" (no scheme), "#f" (no scheme), "?" alone, "#" alone, "/" alone, "//" alone. Also: for a scheme-less input, is a '?'/'#' still split out ("a/b?c#d")? And does the path include a leading '/' always, or can path be non-slash-prefixed after an authority ("http://ex.comfoo" is one host; but check something like "http://ex.com\\p")? Check that query keeps '&', '=', '+', ';' verbatim and fragment keeps everything verbatim. Report the exact substring boundaries.

content.text: I've run ~92 distinct probes. Submitting findings.

rules.rule: MAJOR / ORDERING: the fragment and query are stripped from the ENTIRE raw input BEFORE scheme detection, not after authority parsing. Algorithm: s = argv[1]; i = s.find('#'); if (i != npos) { fragment = s.substr(i+1); s = s.substr(0,i); } j = s.find('?'); if (j != npos) { query = s.substr(j+1); s = s.substr(0,j); } then parse scheme/authority/path from the shortened s. Proof: "http#://ex.com" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, path "http", fragment "://ex.com". The literal "://" is present in the raw input, yet no scheme is found, because it was already moved into the fragment. Same for "ht?tp://ex.com/p" -> path "ht", query "tp://ex.com/p", no scheme.

'#' is located first (over the whole input) and '?' is searched only in the prefix before that '#'. Consequences that hold universally: query() can NEVER contain '#'; fragment() CAN contain both '#' and '?'; path() can contain NEITHER '?' nor '#'. Evidence: "a/b#c?d" -> path "a/b", query "" (has_query 0), fragment "c?d"; "http://ex.com/a?b?c#d#e" -> path "/a", query "b?c", fragment "d#e".

Only the FIRST '#' is a delimiter; every later '#' stays verbatim in the fragment. Only the FIRST '?' in the pre-'#' prefix is a delimiter; every later '?' stays verbatim in the query. Evidence: "a#b#c" -> fragment "b#c"; "a?b?c" -> query "b?c"; "http://ex.com/##" -> fragment "#"; "http://ex.com/??" -> query "?".

Because '?' and '#' are already removed before scheme/authority parsing, the authority region ends at the FIRST '/' in the post-"://" remainder ONLY. The apparent rule "authority ends at first of '/', '?', '#'" is an observational consequence, not a separate check. Implement as: rest = s.substr(pos_of_"://" + 3); k = rest.find('/'); authority_region = (k==npos ? rest : rest.substr(0,k)); path = (k==npos ? "" : rest.substr(k)). Evidence: "http://ex.com?x:80" -> host "ex.com", port -1, query "x:80"; "http://ex#.com/p" -> host "ex", fragment ".com/p"; "http://ex.com:8#0/p" -> host "ex.com", port 8, fragment "0/p".

When a scheme was found ("://" present in the post-strip string), path() is either the empty string (no '/' in the remainder) or a string that ALWAYS begins with '/'. A non-slash-prefixed path after an authority is impossible. Evidence: "http://ex.com" -> path "", has_path 0; "http://ex.com/" -> path "/", has_path 1; "http://ex.com?x" -> path "".

Backslash is NOT a delimiter and does not terminate the authority: "http://ex.com\\p" (one literal backslash) -> host "ex.com\p", authority "ex.com\p", path "", has_path 0, is_valid 1. Only '/' (and the pre-stripped '?'/'#') end the authority region.

The path is taken from the first '/' INCLUSIVE, so extra slashes are preserved and empty authority is possible: "http:///p" -> authority "", has_authority 0, host "", path "/p"; "http:////p" -> authority "", path "//p"; "http://ex.com//a//b" -> path "//a//b".

With NO scheme (no "://" after the '#'/'?' strip), the whole remaining string becomes path() verbatim, including leading slashes; no authority is parsed. Evidence: "/" -> path "/"; "//" -> path "//" (host "", has_authority 0); "a" -> path "a"; "ex.com?q=1" -> path "ex.com", query "q=1"; "/a/./b/../c?x=./y#z/../w" -> path "/a/./b/../c", query "x=./y", fragment "z/../w".

Query/fragment splitting applies EQUALLY to scheme-less input — there is no requirement of a scheme or authority. Evidence: "a/b?c#d" -> path "a/b", query "c", fragment "d"; "?q=1" -> path "", query "q=1"; "#f" -> fragment "f".

An empty piece after a delimiter yields an empty string with the corresponding has_*() == 0, and the delimiter is DROPPED from to_string() (lossy round-trip). Evidence: "http://ex.com/?" -> query "", has_query 0, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "http://ex.com/#" -> fragment "", has_fragment 0, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "http://ex.com/?#" -> both empty, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "?" -> to_string ""; "#" -> to_string "".

has_query() == !query.empty() and has_fragment() == !fragment.empty() and has_path() == !path.empty(). There is no separate "delimiter was present" flag. Evidence: "http://ex.com?#" -> has_query 0, has_fragment 0, identical output to "http://ex.com" except nothing; "http://ex.com/##" -> fragment "#" so has_fragment 1.

path()/query()/fragment() are byte-verbatim substrings: no percent-decoding, no normalization, no case folding, no whitespace trimming. '&', '=', '+', ';', '%', ':', '@', spaces, and tabs all survive. Evidence: "http://ex.com/?a=1&b=2;c+d=e%20f" -> query "a=1&b=2;c+d=e%20f"; "http://ex.com/#a=1&b;c+d%7E" -> fragment "a=1&b;c+d%7E"; "http://ex.com/p;a=1&b=2+c=%7E" -> path "/p;a=1&b=2+c=%7E"; "HTTP://EX.COM/PaTh?Q=A#F" -> path "/PaTh", query "Q=A", fragment "F" (case preserved; only scheme lowercased); "http://ex.com/ ?  # " -> path "/ ", query "  ", fragment " "; "   " -> path "   ", is_valid 1; tab-containing input verified byte-exact via od -c.

'://' at offset 0 produces an EMPTY scheme with has_scheme 0, yet the authority IS still parsed (because a "://" was found). Evidence: "://ex.com" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, authority "ex.com", has_authority 1, host "ex.com", to_string "" ; "://u@ex.com:80/p?q#f" -> userinfo "u", host "ex.com", port 80, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", has_scheme 0, to_string "/p?q#f".

to_string() reconstruction: out = ""; if (has_scheme()) out += scheme + "://" + authority(); if (has_path()) out += path; if (has_query()) out += "?" + query; if (has_fragment()) out += "#" + fragment. Note the authority is emitted ONLY inside the has_scheme branch, so a parsed authority with an empty scheme is silently lost. Evidence: "://ex.com" -> to_string "" despite authority "ex.com"; "://ex.com/p" -> to_string "/p"; "http:///p" -> to_string "http:///p" (scheme + "://" + "" + "/p"); "a://b://c/p" -> to_string "a://b//c/p" (authority region "b:" reconstructed as "b", port dropped).

to_string() is lossy in exactly three ways relevant to this family: (a) an empty query/fragment loses its '?'/'#' delimiter, (b) an authority with no scheme is dropped entirely, (c) an unparseable/empty port loses its ':'. Evidence for (a)+(b) combined: "http://ex.com/?#?#" -> path "/", query "", fragment "?#", to_string "http://ex.com/#?#" (the '?' of the empty query is gone).

is_valid() == has_host() || has_path()  (equivalently: !host.empty() || !path.empty()). Scheme, query and fragment do NOT contribute. Evidence for 1: "/" (path only) -> 1; "a" -> 1; "://ex.com" (host, no scheme, no path) -> 1; "http#://ex.com" (path "http" only) -> 1; "   " -> 1. Evidence for 0: "?q=1" -> 0; "#f" -> 0; "?" -> 0; "#" -> 0; "?#" -> 0; "#?" -> 0; "#/" -> 0 (fragment "/" only); "?/" -> 0; "http://#ex.com" -> has_scheme 1 but host "" and path "" -> 0; "a://" -> 0; "://" -> 0.

has_authority() == has_host() == !host.empty() in every probe run; the reconstructed authority string being non-empty is irrelevant. Evidence: "http:///p" -> authority "", has_authority 0; "://ex.com" -> has_authority 1; "http://ex.com:8#0/p" -> authority "ex.com:8", host "ex.com", has_authority 1; combined with the given fact "http://:8080" -> authority ":8080" but has_authority 0.

evidence.note: No trailing slash -> path is EMPTY, has_path 0
Trailing slash -> path "/", has_path 1. Contrast with previous.
KEY: fragment stripped BEFORE scheme detection, so the "://" is never seen as a scheme delimiter
KEY: '#' split first (frag "://ex.com"), then '?' inside prefix "ht?tp" -> path "ht", query "tp"
Empty scheme (has_scheme 0) but authority IS parsed; to_string drops the authority entirely -> ""
Full authority parsed with empty scheme; to_string emits only path+query+fragment
First '#' at the 2nd-to-last group: frag "?#"; then '?' in prefix -> empty query. to_string LOSES the '?'
Both query and fragment empty -> both has_* 0, both delimiters dropped from to_string
'#' first -> fragment "?" verbatim; no query. Asymmetric with the previous probe.
Scheme-less: '#' wins over later '?'; fragment keeps '?'
Only first delimiter of each kind splits; query keeps '?', fragment keeps '#'
Backslash does NOT end the authority; it becomes part of the host. Path stays empty.
First "://" wins; authority region is "b:" (up to first '/'), path "//c/p"; to_string lossy (colon dropped)
Empty authority, path "/p"; has_authority 0. to_string round-trips exactly.
Path taken from first '/' inclusive, extra slashes preserved
has_scheme 1 but host and path both empty -> is_valid 0. Proves scheme does not confer validity.
'#' cuts mid-port: port region is "8" -> port 8; fragment "0/p"; path empty
':80' is inside the query, never considered as a port
Query keeps &, =, +, ;, %XX verbatim; no decoding
Fragment keeps '/', '?', '&', '=', and further '#' verbatim
Only scheme is lowercased; host, path, query, fragment keep case
Query alone: is_valid 0 (no host, no path)
Fragment alone: is_valid 0
The '/' is inside the fragment, path stays empty -> is_valid 0
Path "/" alone -> is_valid 1
No scheme -> no authority parsing; whole string is path
All fields empty; to_string ""; is_valid 0
Second '#' is literal fragment content
Second '?' is literal query content
Authority ends at the first '/' even though '@' appears later; '@' ends up in the path
No whitespace trimming in path, query, or fragment
No dot-segment normalization anywhere

ambiguities: SURPRISING (but firmly established): the '#'/'?' split runs over the RAW input before the "://" scheme search. This means a '#' or '?' occurring anywhere before the "://" destroys scheme AND authority parsing entirely ("http#://ex.com" has no scheme and no host). Any reimplementation that parses the scheme first and only then splits query/fragment will diverge on these inputs. This is the single highest-risk rule in this family.

SURPRISING: to_string() emits the authority only when has_scheme() is true, so "://ex.com" round-trips to the empty string even though host()/authority() are populated and is_valid() is 1. I could not find any input with an empty scheme whose to_string included the authority.

to_string() is not injective: "http://ex.com", "http://ex.com?", "http://ex.com#", and "http://ex.com?#" all produce to_string "http://ex.com". Likewise "http://ex.com/?#?#" -> "http://ex.com/#?#". So an empty-but-present query/fragment is unrecoverable.

is_valid() == has_host() || has_path() fits all 92 probes, but I could not construct a case that separates it from a possible alternative like "!(host.empty() && path.empty())" plus some scheme condition — every scheme-bearing input I tried with empty host and empty path ("http://", "a://", "http://#ex.com", "http://?ex.com") returned 0, and every input with a non-empty host or path returned 1. Marked 'likely' rather than 'certain' only because the rule is inferred from coincidence across cases rather than from an isolating probe.

has_authority() tracked has_host() exactly in all probes; I never found an input where they differed. It is possible the implementation checks something subtly different (e.g. "host non-empty" vs "authority region contained a host"), but no probe distinguishes them.

I did not test bytes above 0x7F (UTF-8 / raw high bytes) or embedded NUL in the path/query/fragment; NUL cannot be passed through argv at all, and multi-byte behavior is presumed byte-verbatim by analogy with tabs and spaces but was not directly probed.
Very long inputs (length-based truncation or overflow in the splitting code) were not probed.
